title: Flydubai Hijack Suspect Likely Acted Alone, Investigators Say, as Australia Link Emerges
excerpt: Israeli officials say early evidence points to a lone attacker with no established group or state backing, while Australian agencies examine the Omani co-pilot's 2015-2017 residence on a student visa.
body:
• Investigators from multiple countries believe Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking flydubai flight FZ1073 on September 30, likely acted alone, Israeli officials told CNN — though all avenues remain open.
  • The Dubai-to-Tel Aviv Boeing 737 MAX 8 plunged nearly 14,000 feet in under 30 seconds after the co-pilot allegedly attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe; the plane made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
  • UAE Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi has formally called the incident a "terrorist act."
  • Al-Hammami was flagged for extremist views at Oman Air in 2024 and later lived in Australia on a student visa from 2015 to 2017; Australian federal agencies are now examining his former contacts and travel history.

Dubai: The co-pilot accused of attempting to hijack a flydubai passenger jet last week likely acted alone, according to Israeli officials close to the multi-agency investigation — an assessment that narrows, but does not close, one of the most alarming aviation security incidents in recent years.

Early evidence points to an isolated perpetrator with no established organizational ties or foreign state backing, an Israeli official told CNN, in reporting corroborated by CBS News sources. A second Israeli source said that "at the moment, Israel does not know of any link to a group or government." Both officials stressed this is their understanding so far; investigators in the UAE, Israel and Saudi Arabia continue to keep all avenues open.

What happened on September 30

Flight FZ1073, a Boeing 737 MAX 8 from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying 174 passengers — almost all of them Israelis — was over the region on September 30 when co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami allegedly attacked Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian-origin pilot, with the cockpit's emergency crash axe and attempted to seize the controls.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2106930862311014438

The aircraft plunged nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds. Despite his wounds, Captain Machchhar unlocked the reinforced cockpit door and signaled distress; passengers, crew and off-duty flydubai pilots rushed into the cockpit, subdued the attacker and stabilized the plane, which made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

UAE Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi has formally designated the incident a "terrorist act." "Investigations into the incident involving Flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the copilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack," he said, according to the UAE state news agency.

"Investigations into the incident involving Flydubai flight FZ1073 found that the copilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist attack."

— Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, UAE Prosecutor General

A flagged past

Al-Hammami — named by media and intelligence sources but not formally by authorities — was born in the UAE to a Syrian mother and Omani father, and had traveled to Syria. He was flagged over extremist views while employed at Oman Air in 2024: extremist materials were found in his possession and radical ideological views identified, leading to his removal from flying duties and transfer to an administrative role, according to information disclosed to the Associated Press.

He subsequently passed flydubai's standard security checks, which, according to a Gulf diplomat, focused on criminal convictions rather than radicalization. A social media post on one of his accounts included a photo of Ayman al-Zawahiri. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News on October 2 that the suspect "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," citing "personal information" from ongoing questioning.

The incident has also raised questions about pre-flight screening: Israel received the crew list in advance, and scrutiny continues over how al-Hammami was cleared for an Israel-bound flight. US President Donald Trump had earlier suggested, without evidence, that the suspect could be linked to Iran; investigators have found no links to terrorist organizations or foreign-government orders.

The Australia connection

Australian federal agencies have opened inquiries after it emerged that al-Hammami resided in Australia on a student visa between 2015 and 2017. His visa was revoked in 2019 on administrative grounds — non-enrolment — rather than character concerns, and Australian police and partner intelligence services are now scrutinizing his former domestic contacts and travel history from that period.

What next

The joint inquiry across the UAE, Israel, Saudi Arabia and now Australia is expected to examine both the suspect's radicalization path and the screening failures that let a previously flagged pilot into a cockpit. For the aviation industry, the case is already prompting hard questions about how airlines vet crew for ideological risk — checks that, as this case shows, can be the difference between an uneventful flight and a 14,000-foot plunge.
image_caption: A flydubai Boeing 737 in flight. Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv was targeted in an attempted hijacking on September 30, with 174 passengers aboard.
nri_angle: The flight's captain, Smit Machchhar, is of Indian origin and was hailed as a hero for saving 174 passengers — a point of pride and attention for Indian travelers on Gulf routes.
